The Waccamaw silverside Menidia extensa is a small-bodied atheriniform fish endemic to Lake Waccamaw in North Carolina. Newly hatched yolk-sac larvae emerge from the chorion at an extremely small size, with total length at birth measured at 0.7 centimeters [Lb = 0.7 centimeters], a value consistent with the general range reported for Atheriniformes. Under laboratory conditions maintained at a constant 21 °C [T = 21 °C], the developmental interval from ovum activation to hatching is completed in approximately six days [ab = approximately six days], reflecting the rapid embryogenesis typical of this family. During the initial lecithotrophic phase, the prolarva relies entirely on endogenous yolk reserves, and upon reaching the mouth-opening stage it transitions to exogenous feeding. The wet weight at birth is estimated at 0.00022 grams [Wwb = 0.00022 grams], placing newly emerged individuals among the smallest known for freshwater atherinids. This minuscule size influences early survival probabilities and likely constrains the timing of first feeding, as the yolk-sac larva must rapidly develop its visual and locomotory capabilities to capture suitably small zooplankton prey such as rotifers and copepod nauplii.

As individuals grow through the planktonic larval phase and undergo larval-juvenile transformation, their body length increases substantially into the sub-adult stage. The total length at puberty, representing the size at which gonadal maturation commences, has been estimated at 3.5 centimeters [Lp = 3.5 centimeters], a threshold that marks the transition from an immature juvenile to a reproductively viable sub-adult. At this size, the individual reaches a wet weight at puberty of approximately 0.5 grams [Wwp = approximately 0.5 grams], reflecting the somatic investment necessary to support gametogenesis and the onset of vitellogenesis in females. The time since birth at puberty, assessed under stable thermal conditions at 21 °C [T = 21 °C], is approximately one year since birth [tp = approximately one year since birth], a duration that aligns with the annual spawning cycle observed in this species. This pace of sexual maturation is relatively rapid compared to many other freshwater teleosts of similar size, likely an adaptation to the short-lived, seasonal nature of the Lake Waccamaw ecosystem where growing-season length strongly dictates reproductive opportunities.

The attainment of ultimate body size in Menidia extensa is characterized by a deceleration of growth as asymptotic dimensions are approached. Adult individuals reach a maximum total length, or ultimate total length, of 6.5 centimeters [Li = 6.5 centimeters], making this species one of the larger members of the genus Menidia within its restricted geographic range. Corresponding to this length, the ultimate wet weight of fully grown adults is approximately 3.32 grams [Wwi = approximately 3.32 grams], a mass that reflects the allometric relationship between length and body volume typical of slender-bodied atherinids. Comparative data suggest that this asymptotic size is consistent with the energetic constraints imposed by the relatively low productivity of Lake Waccamaw's blackwater habitat, where limited nutrient availability likely curtails the maximum attainable body size. Field surveys indicate that most individuals reach this maximum size within their second year of life, after which growth becomes negligible and energy is primarily channeled into somatic maintenance and reproductive effort.

Reproductive output in the Waccamaw silverside is tightly coupled to the thermal regime of its environment. Under controlled conditions at 21 °C [T = 21 °C], females produce eggs in multiple clutches across an extended spawning season. Each clutch yields approximately 4 to 5 eggs [N_R_i = Each clutch yields approximately 4 to 5 eggs], and gravid individuals are capable of depositing a new clutch roughly every 2 to 3 days [F_R_i = clutch roughly every 2 to 3 days] during peak reproductive activity. This high frequency of spawning events translates into a substantial daily reproductive output, with each female potentially producing around 150 eggs per year [Ri = around 150 eggs per year] under optimal thermal conditions at 21 °C [T = 21 °C]. The maximum reproductive rate is therefore considerable for a fish of this body size, reflecting an iteroparous strategy that spreads reproductive risk across the breeding season. Temperature plays a critical role in modulating this output, as ovarian recrudescence and oocyte maturation are strongly influenced by metabolic rates, which increase predictably at warmer temperatures within the species' tolerance range.

Longevity in Menidia extensa is modest, as is characteristic of many small-bodied atheriniform fishes. The maximum recorded lifespan under natural conditions is approximately three years [am = approximately three years], a duration measured at the typical environmental temperature of 21 °C [T = 21 °C] prevalent in Lake Waccamaw during the active growing season. This relatively short lifespan constrains the total number of spawning seasons available to an individual, making early maturation and high fecundity essential for population persistence. The three-year lifespan places this species among the shorter-lived members of the Menidia genus, likely as an evolutionary response to the stochastic nature of its coastal plain lake habitat, where periodic drought and fluctuations in water level can cause episodic mortality. Senescence in older individuals manifests as reduced condition factor and diminished egg quality, and post-reproductive death typically occurs following the completion of the third spawning season. The life history strategy thus emphasizes rapid growth, early reproduction, and high annual reproductive effort over extended somatic longevity.
